title: Habría or Hubiera? Two Forms in the Result

sections.title: A second form for the result
sections.content: You know *quisiera* from B2 Unit 9, where *quisiera*, *pudiera* and *debiera* stand in for *querría*, *podría* and *debería*: the *-ra* form of the imperfect subjunctive doing the work of a conditional, for three verbs only. In the past the same idea is much wider. In the result clause of a past counterfactual, *hubiera* + past participle can replace *habría* + past participle, and this works with every verb. So *Si hubiera salido antes, habría llegado* and *Si hubiera salido antes, hubiera llegado* mean the same. The second is common in speech and writing across Latin America; the first is the form you can always use. Only the result clause may change: the *si* clause keeps *hubiera* + participle.

sections.title: Two forms, one meaning
rows: Si lo hubiera sabido, habría venido.
If I had known, I would have come.
Si lo hubiera sabido, hubiera venido.
The same meaning: hubiera in both clauses.
Wrong: the conditional never goes after si.
Only three verbs allow the plain -ra form (B2 Unit 9); with hubiera + participle every verb does.

items.spanish: Si me hubieras avisado, te hubiera acompañado al médico.
items.english: If you had told me, I would have gone with you to the doctor.

items.spanish: Si hubiéramos tenido más tiempo, hubiéramos visitado el museo.
items.english: If we had had more time, we would have visited the museum.

items.spanish: Si hubieras estudiado más, habrías aprobado.
items.english: If you had studied more, you would have passed.

sections.content: The second *hubiera* is a result, so it can never follow *si*, and it still needs a past participle: *hubiera venido*, not *hubiera venir*. With simple verbs, keep the conditional: say *Si tuviera tiempo, viajaría*, not *viajara*.
